reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Neurocutaneous disorder characterised by a facial capillary malformation (port-wine birthmark), leptomeningeal angiomatosis, and eye involvement
The facial birthmark typically follows the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and upper facial involvement raises the risk of brain and eye disease
Leptomeningeal angiomatosis predisposes to seizures, which often begin in infancy and can be difficult to control
Stroke-like episodes, hemiparesis, and progressive cognitive impairment may occur from impaired cortical perfusion
Glaucoma is a common ocular complication and requires ongoing monitoring of intraocular pressure
Caused by a somatic mosaic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene arising during early development, so it is not typically inherited
Characteristic tram-track cortical calcification may be seen on imaging in affected brain regions
A port-wine birthmark alone, without brain or eye involvement, does not constitute the full syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene occurring in a subset of cells during early embryogenesis, producing a mosaic distribution that explains the segmental capillary malformations. The mutation dysregulates signalling in vascular and other tissues, leading to abnormal capillary-venous malformations in the skin, leptomeninges, and eye. The leptomeningeal vascular malformation impairs normal venous drainage and cortical perfusion, causing chronic ischaemia, cortical atrophy, calcification, and a lowered seizure threshold. Because the mutation is somatic and mosaic rather than germline, the condition arises sporadically and is not inherited.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated port-wine birthmark without systemic involvement
Other causes of infantile seizures with focal deficits
additionalInvestigations: Brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast to demonstrate leptomeningeal angiomatosis
Regular ophthalmological review including intraocular pressure measurement for glaucoma
Imaging for cortical calcification when clinically indicated
redFlags: Poorly controlled or prolonged seizures requiring urgent treatment to limit neurological injury
Stroke-like episodes with acute focal deficits
Rising intraocular pressure or visual deterioration from glaucoma
Progressive developmental regression signalling worsening cortical involvement
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with the extent of brain and eye involvement; some individuals have well-controlled seizures and near-normal development, while extensive leptomeningeal disease can lead to refractory epilepsy, hemiparesis, and cognitive impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming any facial port-wine birthmark implies the full syndrome without assessing brain and eye involvement
Failing to monitor for glaucoma, which can present at any age
Undertreating early seizures with consequences for development
Not recognising the mosaic somatic cause and incorrectly counselling about heritability
